summary:
Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route. Legal recognition now covers historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition pathway. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Human Rights Watch and activists including Akkai Padmashali describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, and the BBC reports critics saying it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender; independent estimates put the population at about two million.

Identity documents are a live friction point. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person whom passport authorities had required to undergo a medical examination. In November 2024 airport security personnel stopped an openly transgender law student at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 even though she presented her PAN card. A trans woman in Kolkata alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at a station under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading treatment in custody. The UK government's December 2025 policy note assesses reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, more likely in conservative rural areas, and not systemic.

The constitutional baseline offers protection. The Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that reasoning in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018. India has no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, and courts have recognised same-sex couples as family units, which leaves a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status without a route to local marital recognition. In June 2021 the Madras High Court, in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, issued guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ people from police harassment, ordered police sensitisation, banned conversion therapy, and directed the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

The replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans people from sexual violence. Trans people report fearing a rise in assaults as a result, which bears directly on how a complaint of sexual violence would be framed and received.

Transition-related healthcare sits in a mixed framework. The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for members of the transgender community. Conversion therapy is banned under the 2021 Madras High Court ruling and a 2022 National Medical Commission measure, though clandestine networks continue to operate nationwide. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance confirmed that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is contested and shifting. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 59 per cent of respondents still describe homosexuality as morally unacceptable; a 2023 Gallup poll found 53 per cent support for same-sex marriage; a 2021 Ipsos survey of urban internet users found 17 per cent identifying as non-heterosexual or non-cisgender.

Conservative organisations including the Vishva Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal have labelled same-sex marriage a Western attack on Indian culture and have occasionally targeted Pride events.

Demographic studies cited in the source inventory report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities. No figures disaggregated for trans people accompany that finding, and no trans-specific homicide rate is available for comparison against the general crime rate.
localsOnly:
Welfare delivery is largely state-level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

In higher education the University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. IIT Delhi and IIT Bombay host trans support groups, Indradhanu and Saathi, and American College in Madurai teaches genderqueer and intersex human rights curricula drawing on the work of the transgender activists A. Revathi and Kalki Subramaniam.

Intersex minors face coercive medical intervention. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, which led the Madras High Court in April 2019 to order Tamil Nadu to ban sex-selective surgery on intersex infants.

Community organisations including GayBombay, Good as You in Bangalore and Sappho for Equality in Kolkata operate alongside Pride events held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999. Transgender people hold public office: Shabnam Mausi became the first transgender elected official in 1998, and transgender mayors and judges have since taken office. Menaka Guruswamy became the first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament in March 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document how the 2026 recognition categories are being applied in practice at state welfare boards, or whether documents issued to people recognised under the 2019 law remain valid after the amendment.

It is unresolved whether passport or airport identity procedures will change in response to the February 2026 Allahabad High Court case, and how frequently passport authorities demand medical examination of trans applicants.

Trans-specific violence data disaggregated from general crime statistics are not sourced, and no figure is available on prosecutions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita where a trans complainant is involved.
